name: Tim Hecker
label: Kranky
lede: A government policy analyst turned PhD in noise who dragged pipe organs through distortion, put a falling piano on a record cover and spent twenty years arguing that ambient music should never be background.

eras.title: Jetone, and a government day job
eras.text: Born in Vancouver in 1974 to two art teachers, Tim Hecker played in high-school rock bands before a sampler pulled him toward electronics. He made techno as Jetone, moved to Montreal, and started releasing drifting, crackling records under his own name while working for the Canadian government.

years.h: Tim Hecker debuts as the techno producer Jetone
years.p: Hecker's first releases come under the alias Jetone, on labels in the orbit of German experimental techno such as Mille Plateaux and Force Inc.

years.h: Tim Hecker moves from Vancouver to Montreal for Concordia
years.p: Hecker relocates to study at Concordia University. Montreal becomes his base for the next two decades.

years.h: Haunt Me, Haunt Me Do It Again: the first record as Tim Hecker
years.p: Disenchanted with the direction of Jetone, Hecker releases his debut under his own name on Montreal's Alien8 Recordings.
years.xp: In the early 2000s Hecker was also working as a policy analyst for the Canadian government, making records on the side of a civil-service career. He kept the job until 2006.

years.h: Radio Amor: an album about a Honduran shrimp fisherman
years.p: Recorded in Montreal and Halifax in 2001–02 and released on Mille Plateaux, the album grew from Tim Hecker's 1990s trip to Honduras and a fisherman named Jimmy he met there.
years.xp: Hecker said he was totally obsessed with the idea of fishermen in the Caribbean. Pitchfork's Mark Richardson called Radio Amor his coldest and most piercing work. Alien8 reissued it in 2007 and Kranky did again in 2018.

years.h: Mirages: Tim Hecker's heaviest Alien8 record
years.p: The third Tim Hecker album, on Alien8. He later described Harmony in Ultraviolet as keeping the heaviness of Mirages while adding melody.

eras.title: Quitting the government for organ and static
eras.text: In 2006 Tim Hecker left his government job, enrolled in a PhD at McGill and joined the Chicago drone label Kranky. His first album there, built from pipe organ and guitar run through distortion, is still the one critics reach for.

years.h: Tim Hecker quits his policy job to start a PhD at McGill
years.p: Hecker's doctoral thesis on urban noise, published in 2014 as The era of megaphonics: on the productivity of loud sound, 1880–1930, led to a lectureship in sound culture at McGill.

years.cap: Harmony in Ultraviolet, Kranky, 2006. Cover: the Monument to Fallen Partisans, Bologna
years.h: Harmony in Ultraviolet: Tim Hecker's first album for Kranky
years.p: Recorded in Montreal and Banff, it runs pipe organ, guitars and strings through distortion. Pitchfork later ranked it the ninth best ambient album of all time.
years.xp:
The title riffs on Henri Matisse's painting Harmony in Red, with ultraviolet picked because it can't be seen. Hecker shot the cover himself: the Monument to Fallen Partisans in Bologna's Piazza Maggiore, a memorial to the Italian Resistance, chosen for its crude qualities.

Tracks like Radio Spiricom, named for a 1980s device that claimed to talk to the dead, and the 13-minute Whitecaps of White Noise suite made the record loud and dense for an ambient album. Pitchfork gave it 8.7 and made it the 14th best album of 2006.

years.h: An Imaginary Country on Kranky
years.p: Tim Hecker's second Kranky album, around the time he was touring with [[Godspeed You! Black Emperor|3648db01-b29d-4ab9-835c-83f6a5068fe4]] and [[Sigur Rós|f6f2326f-6b25-4170-b89d-e235b25508e8]].

eras.title: One day in a Reykjavík church
eras.text: With Ben Frost as engineer and co-conspirator, Tim Hecker recorded a pipe organ in an Icelandic church in a single day and spent months tearing it apart. Ravedeath, 1972 won a Juno, and Virgins became his best-reviewed record.

years.h: Tim Hecker and Ben Frost record the organ at Fríkirkjan, Reykjavík
years.p: Ben Frost found the church. In one day Hecker tracked its pipe organ plus guitar and piano, then took the tapes home to Montreal and Banff to rebuild them.

q: the wrongest and the most right title ever
years.h: Ravedeath, 1972 and the MIT piano drop on its cover
years.p: Tim Hecker's Kranky album (krank154) puts a 1972 photo of MIT students pushing a piano off Baker House on the cover. It wins the Juno for Electronic Album of the Year.
years.xp:
Hecker licensed the photo from MIT's archives and re-photographed it, inspired by images of mass media being destroyed, like pirated DVDs crushed by bulldozers. The track titles keep the theme going: The Piano Drop, Hatred of Music, Studio Suicide, 1980.

Metacritic scored it 86. It was longlisted for the Polaris Prize, placed third on The Quietus's 2011 list, and later landed at No. 136 on Pitchfork's 200 best albums of the 2010s.

years.h: Instrumental Tourist with Oneohtrix Point Never's Daniel Lopatin
years.p: [[Daniel Lopatin|d5cd6528-3185-4f1b-a297-807b00b16f83]] proposed the team-up. Days of improvising at Mexican Summer's studio were edited down, Teo Macero style, and released on Lopatin's Software label.
years.xp: The two had admired each other's work without ever meeting formally. Hecker said the album took shape almost unconsciously, through joking around.

years.h: Virgins: a shrouded statue and an Abu Ghraib echo
years.p: Recorded in Reykjavík, Seattle and Troy, New York, with woodwinds, piano and synths. The cover, shot by Tim Hecker in Milan Cathedral, shows a Virgin Mary covered for restoration, echoing a famous Abu Ghraib photo.
years.xp: Hecker described the record's rhythmic, staccato, aggressive blasts as deliberately hostile to the ambient label. With [[Kara-Lis Coverdale|aabe385c-379a-467f-9a6d-2560ffa0b730]], [[Valgeir Sigurðsson|b47171a4-1bfc-4d80-a91e-33c368fa6a5a]] and Ben Frost playing, it scored 87 on Metacritic, his best ever, placed fifth in The Wire's critics' poll and was longlisted for the 2014 Polaris Prize.

eras.title: A detour to 4AD and a Tokyo temple
eras.text: Tim Hecker finished his doctorate, signed to 4AD, worked with a choir scored by Jóhann Jóhannsson, then went back to Kranky for two records made with a Japanese gagaku ensemble. Film directors started calling.

years.h: Love Streams: 4AD, Icelandic choir, liturgy after Yeezus
years.p: Signed to 4AD that February, Tim Hecker recorded in Reykjavík with the Icelandic Choir Ensemble, vocals arranged by Jóhann Jóhannsson. His stated themes: liturgical aesthetics after Yeezus, and the voice in the age of auto-tune.

years.h: Tim Hecker scores The Free World for Sundance
years.p: His first feature score is for Jason Lew's drama, selected for the 2016 Sundance U.S. Dramatic Competition.

years.h: Konoyo: Tim Hecker records with gagaku players in a Tokyo temple
years.p: Back on Kranky, Hecker built the album from sessions with the Tokyo Gakuso ensemble at Jiunzan Mandala-Temple Kanzouin outside Tokyo, with shō, hichiriki and ryuteki woodwinds.
years.xp: Cellist Mariel Roberts and Kara-Lis Coverdale also play, with Ben Frost engineering. Metacritic scored it 81, and it reached No. 18 on the UK Dance Albums chart.

years.h: Anoyo: the second record from the Konoyo sessions
years.p: Konoyo means this world; Anoyo, the other world, completes Tim Hecker's pair of gagaku records.

eras.title: Against the wellness playlist
eras.text: Through the pandemic Tim Hecker took up Buddhism and meditated in his studio, scored a BBC drama and a Brandon Cronenberg horror film, and made an album aimed squarely at the soothing ambient filling streaming playlists.

years.h: Tim Hecker, a former Catholic, turns to Buddhism
years.p: During the COVID-19 pandemic Hecker began studying Buddhism and practicing meditation in his studio.

years.h: Scores for BBC's The North Water and Austria's Luzifer
years.p: Tim Hecker scores Andrew Haigh's Arctic whaling drama and Peter Brunner's Luzifer, which won Franz Rogowski best actor at Fantastic Fest.

years.h: Tim Hecker scores Brandon Cronenberg's Infinity Pool
years.p: The sci-fi horror film with Alexander Skarsgård and Mia Goth premieres at Sundance 2023 with Hecker's score.

years.h: No Highs: Tim Hecker against corporate ambient
years.p: The Kranky press release pitched it as a beacon of unease against false positive corporate ambient. [[Colin Stetson|22b2f6dc-fcc2-490d-a462-f972a692ce12]] plays saxophone on Total Garbage and Monotony II.

years.h: Shards EP
years.p: Tim Hecker's latest release, an EP.
